purpose: Historical evidence supplied to the alternate-present generator. A researched history of Silicon Valley and computing as institutions, capital, networks, and openness from which the model may retain, alter, displace, or build upon events after a user-specified divergence. Dates are established historical record; descriptions are the author's plain summaries.

events.label: Federal Telegraph Corporation
events.description: Founded near Stanford with university backing and a Navy contract, Federal Telegraph seeds the Bay Area's radio-electronics industry and the university-industry-military bond.

events.label: De Forest's Vacuum Tube Amplifier
events.description: At Federal Telegraph, Lee de Forest develops the triode vacuum-tube amplifier, enabling long-distance telephony and radio broadcast — the electronic amplification the whole industry is built on.

events.label: Terman Pushes Students Toward Startups
events.description: Stanford's Frederick Terman encourages his engineering students to found local companies rather than leave for the East Coast, deliberately cultivating a regional startup culture.

events.label: Hewlett-Packard Founded
events.description: Bill Hewlett and David Packard start HP in a Palo Alto garage on Terman's encouragement — later mythologized as the origin story of the garage startup.

events.label: WWII Electronic Warfare Research
events.description: Wartime radar and electronic-warfare research (much of it routed through Terman) floods universities with federal money and trains a generation of Bay Area engineers.

events.label: Varian Associates
events.description: The Varian brothers commercialize the klystron microwave tube, founding a defense-electronics firm that becomes an anchor tenant of the coming Stanford park.

events.label: The Transistor (Bell Labs)
events.description: Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley invent the transistor at Bell Labs on the East Coast — the solid-state device that will later draw Shockley west and give the Valley its silicon.

events.label: Stanford Industrial Park
events.description: Terman spearheads leasing Stanford land to high-tech firms (Varian first, then HP), fusing the university, industry, and real estate into a durable innovation cluster.

events.label: Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory
events.description: William Shockley moves to Mountain View to build silicon transistors, bringing solid-state expertise — and a management style that soon drives his best people out.

events.label: The Traitorous Eight / Fairchild
events.description: Eight of Shockley's engineers — including Noyce and Moore — quit to found Fairchild Semiconductor, establishing the Valley pattern of talent defecting to launch rivals.

events.label: The Integrated Circuit
events.description: Kilby (TI) and Noyce (Fairchild) independently invent the integrated circuit; early demand comes largely from military and Apollo programs.

events.label: Moore's Law
events.description: Gordon Moore observes that transistor counts double roughly every two years, giving the industry a self-fulfilling roadmap and a culture of relentless scaling.

events.label: Intel Founded
events.description: Noyce and Moore leave Fairchild to found Intel with Arthur Rock's venture money — a template for VC-backed semiconductor startups.

events.label: ARPANET / SRI Node
events.description: The first ARPANET message is sent to a node at Stanford Research Institute; the military-funded packet network becomes the internet's backbone.

events.label: Xerox PARC
events.description: Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center invents the personal-computing paradigm — GUI, mouse, Ethernet, laser printer, WYSIWYG — that others will commercialize.

events.label: Intel 4004 Microprocessor
events.description: Intel ships the first commercial single-chip microprocessor, putting a computer's brain on one chip and enabling the personal computer.

events.label: 'Silicon Valley' Coined
events.description: Don Hoefler's trade-press series 'Silicon Valley U.S.A.' names the region, giving the cluster an identity and a mythology.

events.label: Atari / Pong
events.description: Nolan Bushnell's Atari turns the video game into a consumer industry, seeding both the games business and (via employee Steve Jobs) the personal-computer one.

events.label: Sequoia & Kleiner Perkins Founded
events.description: Don Valentine's Sequoia and Eugene Kleiner's Kleiner Perkins formalize Sand Hill Road venture capital, the financing engine of every later boom.

events.label: Xerox Alto / Ethernet
events.description: PARC's Alto is the first computer designed around a GUI and networked by Ethernet — a working personal computer years before the market existed.

events.label: Homebrew Computer Club
events.description: Hobbyists gather in Menlo Park to share designs for the Altair and its successors — an open, amateur culture out of which Apple and much of the PC industry emerge.

events.label: Apple Founded
events.description: Jobs and Wozniak found Apple to sell the Apple I, turning the hobbyist personal computer into a consumer product.

events.label: Genentech (Biotech)
events.description: Genentech founds the biotechnology industry on recombinant DNA and Kleiner Perkins money, showing the Valley's VC model could seed fields beyond electronics.

events.label: Apple II
events.description: The Apple II brings a friendly, expandable personal computer to homes and schools, one of the machines that makes computing a mass consumer good.

events.label: VisiCalc (the Killer App)
events.description: The first spreadsheet turns the personal computer into an indispensable business tool, proving software could sell hardware.

events.label: Genentech IPO
events.description: Genentech's blockbuster IPO with no product on the market inaugurates the pattern of vast public valuations for pre-revenue technology companies.

events.label: Sun Microsystems & SGI
events.description: Sun ('the network is the computer') and Silicon Graphics build the networked workstations that power engineering, the internet, and computer graphics.

events.label: Adobe Founded
events.description: Ex-PARC engineers found Adobe; PostScript and later Photoshop and PDF make the Valley the gatekeeper of professional digital media production.

events.label: The Macintosh
events.description: The Macintosh brings PARC's graphical interface to a mass consumer product, defining how ordinary people would use computers for decades.

events.label: Cisco Systems
events.description: Stanford spinout Cisco commercializes the multiprotocol router, building the plumbing that lets the internet scale.

events.label: The World Wide Web
events.description: Tim Berners-Lee's open Web (from CERN, not the Valley) becomes the medium the Valley will rush to commercialize.

events.label: Linux / Free Software
events.description: Linux and the GNU/free-software movement establish open-source as a rival mode of production to proprietary Valley software — much of the internet ends up running on it.

events.label: Mosaic / Netscape
events.description: The Mosaic browser and then Netscape make the Web usable by everyone and ignite the commercial internet.

events.label: Yahoo, eBay, Amazon
events.description: Directories, marketplaces, and online retail turn the Web into commerce, establishing the consumer-internet business.

events.label: Netscape IPO
events.description: Netscape's soaring IPO with little revenue launches the dot-com boom and the growth-over-profit financing logic.

events.label: Google Founded
events.description: Two Stanford PhD students build a better search engine and, with AdWords, invent the attention-and-advertising business model that will fund the modern internet.

events.label: PayPal / the 'PayPal Mafia'
events.description: PayPal's online payments succeed and its alumni (Musk, Thiel, Hoffman, and others) go on to found or fund much of the next Valley generation.

events.label: Salesforce / Software as a Service
events.description: Salesforce pioneers renting software over the network instead of selling it — the subscription, cloud-tenancy model that reshapes how software is owned.

events.label: The Dot-Com Crash
events.description: The speculative internet bubble bursts, wiping out trillions and thinning the field — but leaving behind the fiber, talent, and survivors of the next era.

events.label: Wikipedia
events.description: A free, volunteer-written encyclopedia shows that mass amateur collaboration can produce a reference work rivaling professional ones — open authorship at scale.

events.label: SpaceX & Tesla
events.description: Musk extends Valley venture logic into rockets and electric cars, pulling hardware and heavy industry back into the startup model.

events.label: Facebook
events.description: Facebook builds the social graph into the dominant attention platform, monetizing personal life through advertising at planetary scale.

events.label: YouTube
events.description: YouTube lets anyone publish video to everyone, breaking the professional gate on moving-image distribution and creating the creator economy.

events.label: Amazon Web Services
events.description: AWS rents computing by the hour, making it possible to start a global service with no servers — and concentrating the internet's infrastructure in a few clouds.

events.label: iPhone & App Store
events.description: The iPhone and App Store put a networked computer in every pocket and route software through a gatekept, revenue-shared platform.

events.label: Airbnb & Uber (Platform Economy)
events.description: Smartphone platforms turn homes and cars into on-demand services, extending Valley intermediation into the physical economy.

events.label: Andreessen Horowitz
events.description: a16z rewrites venture capital as a founder-services brand ('software is eating the world'), intensifying the capital arms race.

events.label: Bitcoin
events.description: Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin proposes money and record-keeping without a central custodian — a challenge to platform custody that the Valley both fights and absorbs.

events.label: Instagram / Mobile Social
events.description: Camera-first mobile social apps make image-sharing the dominant everyday medium and are acquired into the ad platforms.

events.label: The Zero-Interest-Rate Era
events.description: A decade of cheap money floods startups with capital, inflating valuations, subsidizing growth-before-profit, and enabling the 'blitzscaling' unicorn.

events.label: Deep Learning Breakthrough (AlexNet)
events.description: AlexNet's ImageNet win, running on GPUs, ignites the deep-learning boom that becomes the Valley's next platform.

events.label: OpenAI Founded
events.description: OpenAI is founded (nominally as an open nonprofit) to build artificial general intelligence, later pivoting to a capped-profit model backed by Microsoft.

events.label: Founder Reckonings (Uber, WeWork)
events.description: High-profile ousters of founders like Travis Kalanick, and later Adam Neumann, mark limits on the founder-king model even amid abundant capital.

events.label: Nvidia and the Compute Chokepoint
events.description: Nvidia's GPUs become the scarce, decisive input for AI, making a chip company one of the most valuable firms on earth and concentrating power over who can train models.

events.label: The Generative-AI Boom
events.description: ChatGPT and its rivals trigger a capital and talent surge into generative AI, positioning models as the next dominant platform and reopening every question about authorship, custody, and access.

events.label: AI Consolidation (Big Tech + Labs)
events.description: The largest incumbents fund and absorb the leading AI labs, concentrating the new medium's infrastructure and talent inside a handful of companies.
